subject: Biology
summary: Covers foundational principles of ecosystem structure, primary & secondary productivity, detrital decomposition, energy flow dynamics, trophic organization, and ecological pyramids: Ecosystem structural matrix (A.G. Tansley 1935, abiotic & biotic components); Forest vertical stratification (Canopy, Understory, Herb layer, Forest floor); Primary vs Secondary Productivity (GPP vs NPP: NPP = GPP - R, representing usable biomass for heterotrophs); Global biospheric productivity distribution (170 Billion Tonnes total: Terrestrial ecosystems 115 BT [67.6%] vs Oceanic ecosystems 55 BT [32.4%] due to euphotic zone <200m light limits and N/P/Fe nutrient deficiencies; Rainforests/Estuaries highest, Deserts/Abyssal lowest); Five-step decomposition pathway (Fragmentation by detritivores, Leaching of soluble salts, Catabolism by extracellular fungal/bacterial enzymes, Humification forming resistant Humus, and Mineralization releasing inorganic ions); Decomposition regulation (Slow with lignin/chitin/suberin, cold <10°C, and anaerobiosis producing peat; Fast with warm >25°C, moisture, nitrogen/sugars); Energy flow mechanics and thermodynamics (50% PAR at 400-700 nm, 2-10% plant PAR capture [1-5% total]); Lindeman's 10% law (1942, 90% metabolic heat loss R limiting chains to 3-5 trophic levels); Grazing (GFC) vs Detritus (DFC) food chains (GFC dominant in aquatic ecosystems; DFC dominant in terrestrial forests carrying >90% of energy flow); Standing Crop (living biomass dry weight g/m²) vs Standing State (inorganic soil nutrients N, P, K, Ca); Ecological pyramids (Pyramid of Numbers upright in grasslands but inverted in single tree ecosystems; Pyramid of Biomass upright in forests but inverted in open seas due to phytoplankton rapid turnover; Pyramid of Energy ALWAYS UPRIGHT without exception); and Limitations of Eltonian pyramids (assumes simple chains, ignores multi-trophic omnivores, completely excludes decomposers/saprotrophs).

sections.title: Ecosystem Structure & Forest Stratification
sections.topic: A.G. Tansley, Abiotic & Biotic Matrix, & 4-Layer Forest Stratification

summaryBox.title: Quick Section Summary
summaryBox.takeaway: An ecosystem integrates abiotic and biotic components. Stratification layers plant species vertically (Canopy, Understory, Herb layer, Forest floor) to optimize light capture.

sections.codeSnippet:
ECOSYSTEM STRUCTURAL MATRIX
                                         │
         ┌───────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────┐
         ▼                                                               ▼
  ABIOTIC COMPONENTS                                            BIOTIC COMPONENTS
  ├── Climatic Regime (Light, Temp, Water)                      ├── Producers / Autotrophs (T₁)
  ├── Inorganic Nutrients (N, P, K, Ca)                         ├── Consumers / Heterotrophs (T₂, T₃, T₄)
  └── Organic Matrix (Humus, Carbohydrates)                     └── Decomposers / Saprotrophs
sections.content:
### 1.1 Ecosystem & Stratification
- **Ecosystem**: Functional unit of nature (*Tansley 1935*).
- **Forest Stratification**: Canopy $\rightarrow$ Understory $\rightarrow$ Herb Layer $\rightarrow$ Forest Floor.

sections.title: Primary & Secondary Productivity: GPP vs NPP
sections.topic: Gross Primary Productivity, Autotrophic Respiration Losses R, Net Primary Productivity, & Secondary Productivity

summaryBox.title: Quick Section Summary
summaryBox.takeaway: Gross Primary Productivity (GPP) is total photosynthetic carbon fixed. Subtracting autotrophic respiration (R) gives Net Primary Productivity (NPP = GPP - R).

sections.codeSnippet:
GROSS vs NET PRIMARY PRODUCTIVITY
                    
   GROSS PRIMARY PRODUCTIVITY (GPP) ──► Total rate of organic matter synthesis during photosynthesis.
                                               │
   Autotrophic Respiration Losses (R) ◄──────┘
                                               │
   NET PRIMARY PRODUCTIVITY (NPP)   ──► Organic biomass remaining available to Heterotrophs.
sections.content:
### 2.1 Productivity Types
- **Formula**: $\text{NPP} = \text{GPP} - R$.
- **Heterotrophic Supply**: NPP is the biomass available to consumers.
- **Secondary Productivity**: Biomass synthesis by consumers.

sections.title: Global Productivity & Marine Limitations
sections.topic: 170 Billion Tonnes Biosphere NPP, Land vs Ocean Distribution, Euphotic Zone & Nutrient Deficits

summaryBox.title: Quick Section Summary
summaryBox.takeaway: Total biosphere NPP is 170 Billion Tonnes. Land produces 115 BT (67.6%), while Oceans produce only 55 BT (32.4%) due to light limits (<200 m) and nutrient deficits (N, P, Fe).

sections.codeSnippet:
GLOBAL NPP DISTRIBUTION
                      
   TERRESTRIAL ECOSYSTEMS (30% Surface Area) ──► Contributes 115 Billion Tonnes (67.6%)
   OCEANIC ECOSYSTEMS    (70% Surface Area) ──► Contributes ONLY 55 Billion Tonnes (32.4%)
sections.content:
### 3.1 Global NPP Metrics
- **Total**: $170\text{ Billion Tonnes}$.
- **Land vs Oceans**: Land ($115\text{ BT}$, $67.6\%$) vs Oceans ($55\text{ BT}$, $32.4\%$).
- **Extremes**: Tropical rainforests/estuaries highest; Deserts/abyssal lowest.

sections.title: The 5-Step Decomposition Pathway

summaryBox.title: Quick Section Summary
summaryBox.takeaway: Decomposition follows 5 steps: Fragmentation by detritivores, Leaching of soluble salts, Catabolism by microbial enzymes, Humification forming resistant Humus, and Mineralization releasing ions.

sections.codeSnippet:
THE FIVE DECOMPOSITION STEPS
                                    │
  1. FRAGMENTATION ──► Detritivores (Earthworms) break detritus into small particles.
  2. LEACHING      ──► Water-soluble inorganic nutrients sink into soil horizons.
  3. CATABOLISM    ──► Bacterial & fungal enzymes digest complex organic polymers.
  4. HUMIFICATION  ──► Formation of dark, amorphous, resistant Humus.
  5. MINERALIZATION──► Microbial breakdown of humus to release inorganic mineral ions.
sections.content:
### 4.1 Decomposition Steps
- **1. Fragmentation**: Detritivores (*earthworms*).
- **2. Leaching**: Water washes nutrients into soil.
- **3. Catabolism**: Bacterial/fungal enzymes.
- **4. Humification**: Forms dark, colloidal **Humus**.
- **5. Mineralization**: Releases mineral ions ($\text{Ca}^{2+}, \text{Mg}^{2+}, \text{NH}_4^+$).

sections.title: Factors Regulating Decomposition & Peat Formation
sections.topic: Substrate Chemistry (Lignin, Chitin, Nitrogen), Climatic Variables (Temp, Moisture, Oxygen), & Peat Bogs

summaryBox.title: Quick Section Summary
summaryBox.takeaway: Decomposition is accelerated by warm, moist, aerobic conditions and nitrogen-rich substrates; it is inhibited by cold, lignin/chitin, and anaerobiosis (which forms peat).

sections.codeSnippet:
DECOMPOSITION RATE REGULATION
                                      │
         ┌────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────┐
         ▼                                                         ▼
   SUBSTRATE CHEMISTRY                                       CLIMATIC REGIME
   ├── SLOW: Rich in Lignin, Chitin, & Suberin               ├── FAST: Warm (>25°C) & Moist
   └── FAST: Rich in Nitrogen & Water-Soluble Sugars         └── SLOW: Cold (<10°C) & Anaerobiosis
sections.content:
### 5.1 Regulators of Decomposition
- **Substrate**: Lignin/Chitin/Suberin (Slow) vs Nitrogen/Sugars (Fast).
- **Climate**: Warm, moist, aerobic (Fast) vs Cold & Anaerobic (Slow $\rightarrow$ **Peat**).

sections.title: Energy Flow: Thermodynamics & PAR Capture
sections.topic: Unidirectional Energy Flow, 1st & 2nd Laws of Thermodynamics, PAR (400-700 nm), & 2-10% Capture Efficiency

summaryBox.title: Quick Section Summary
summaryBox.takeaway: Energy flow is strictly unidirectional. Plants capture only 2-10% of Photosynthetically Active Radiation (PAR: 400-700 nm), representing 1-5% of total incident sunlight.

sections.codeSnippet:
SOLAR RADIATION CAPTURE
                       
   Incident Solar Radiation ──► 50% is Photosynthetically Active Radiation (PAR: 400–700 nm)
                                             │
   Producers capture ONLY 2–10% of PAR (1–5% of Total Incident Radiation)
sections.content:
### 6.1 Energy Flow & PAR
- **Thermodynamics**: Unidirectional flow; continuous entropy loss via respiratory heat ($R$).
- **PAR**: $50\%$ of incident solar radiation; plants capture **$2\text{--}10\%$ of PAR**.

sections.title: Lindeman's 10% Energy Transfer Law
sections.topic: Raymond Lindeman (1942), 10% Trophic Efficiency, 90% Metabolic Loss, & Food Chain Length Limits

summaryBox.title: Quick Section Summary
summaryBox.takeaway: Lindeman's 10% Law states only ~10% of energy transfers to the next trophic level. 90% is lost as metabolic heat (R), capping natural food chains at 3-5 trophic levels.

sections.codeSnippet:
10% TROPHIC ENERGY PYRAMID
                      
   Tertiary Consumer (T₄)   ──►   1 J
   Secondary Consumer (T₃)  ──►   10 J
   Primary Consumer (T₂)    ──►   100 J
   Primary Producer (T₁)    ──►   1,000 J
   Incident Solar PAR       ──►   100,000 J
sections.content:
### 7.1 Lindeman's 10% Law
- **Efficiency**: $\text{Trophic Efficiency} \approx 10\%$.
- **Calculation**: $1000\text{ J } (T_1) \rightarrow 100\text{ J } (T_2) \rightarrow 10\text{ J } (T_3) \rightarrow 1\text{ J } (T_4)$.
- **Chain Limits**: Restricts food chains to $3\text{--}5\text{ levels}$.

sections.title: Grazing vs Detritus Food Chains: GFC vs DFC
sections.topic: Trophic Levels (T1-T4), GFC in Aquatic Ecosystems, & DFC in Terrestrial Forests

summaryBox.title: Quick Section Summary
summaryBox.takeaway: Grazing Food Chains (GFC) start with living autotrophs and dominate aquatic biomes. Detritus Food Chains (DFC) start with dead detritus and dominate terrestrial forests (>90% energy flow).

sections.codeSnippet:
GRAZING vs DETRITUS FOOD CHAINS
                       
   GRAZING FOOD CHAIN (GFC):  Producers (T₁) ──► Herbivores (T₂) ──► Carnivores (T₃)
                              (Major energy conduit in AQUATIC Ecosystems)
                              
   DETRITUS FOOD CHAIN (DFC): Dead Detritus ──► Saprophytic Fungi/Bacteria ──► Detritivores
                              (Major energy conduit in TERRESTRIAL Ecosystems)
sections.content:
### 8.1 GFC vs DFC
- **GFC**: Producers $\rightarrow$ Herbivores $\rightarrow$ Carnivores (Dominates **Aquatic**).
- **DFC**: Detritus $\rightarrow$ Microbes $\rightarrow$ Detritivores (Dominates **Terrestrial**).

sections.title: Standing Crop vs Standing State
sections.topic: Living Biomass (Dry Weight), Inorganic Soil Nutrients (N, P, K, Ca), & Turnover Rates

summaryBox.title: Quick Section Summary
summaryBox.takeaway: Standing Crop is the total living organic biomass (dry weight, g/m²) at a specific time. Standing State is the total quantity of abiotic inorganic nutrients (N, P, K, Ca) in the soil.

sections.codeSnippet:
BIOTIC vs ABIOTIC ECOSYSTEM POOLS
                         
   STANDING CROP  ──► Total mass of LIVING BIOMASS (Dry Weight in g/m²)
                      or total count of living organisms at a specific time.
                      
   STANDING STATE ──► Total amount of INORGANIC NUTRIENTS (N, P, K, Ca)
                      present in the soil / abiotic reservoir at a given time.
sections.content:
### 9.1 Standing Crop vs State
- **Standing Crop**: Total **living biomass** (dry weight in $\text{g/m}^2$).
- **Standing State**: Total **inorganic nutrients** ($\text{N, P, K, Ca}$) in soil.

sections.title: Ecological Pyramids: Numbers, Biomass, & Energy
sections.topic: Eltonian Pyramids, Upright vs Inverted Models, Inverted Marine Biomass, & Inverted Tree Numbers

summaryBox.title: Quick Section Summary
summaryBox.takeaway: Numbers pyramid inverts in single tree systems; Biomass pyramid inverts in open oceans (phytoplankton rapid turnover); Energy pyramid is ALWAYS upright without exception.

sections.codeSnippet:
INVERTED PYRAMIDS EXAMPLES
                     
   1. INVERTED BIOMASS (Sea)                  2. INVERTED NUMBERS (Tree)
   
      Fishes / T₂ (12 g/m²)                     Hyper-parasites / T₃ (10,000)
      ─────────────────────────                 ─────────────────────────
      Phytoplankton / T₁ (4 g/m²)               Insects / T₂ (1,000)
      ─────────────────                         ───────────────
                                                Single Tree / T₁ (1)
                                                ───────
sections.content:
### 10.1 Ecological Pyramids
- **Numbers**: Upright (Grassland), Inverted (Single Tree).
- **Biomass**: Upright (Forest), **Inverted (Open Ocean/Sea)**.
- **Energy**: **ALWAYS UPRIGHT** without exception.

sections.title: Limitations of Pyramids & High-Yield NEST Traps
sections.topic: Three Pyramidal Limitations, Exclusion of Decomposers, & Master Ecosystem Glossary

summaryBox.title: Quick Section Summary
summaryBox.takeaway: Eltonian pyramids assume linear chains, fail for omnivorous species, and completely exclude decomposers. Master ecosystem glossary and 10 NEST diagnostic traps.

sections.content:
### 11.1 Pyramidal Limitations & Traps
- **Limitations**: Linear chains only, ignores multi-trophic species, **excludes decomposers**.
- **Energy Pyramid**: Never inverted in nature.
- **Marine Biomass**: Inverted due to high phytoplankton turnover.
